changes.summary: The family was by no means an immutable model and evolved throughout the 19th century in line with the era’s political, social and moral disruptions. Regulated by the Civil Code, upheld by the bourgeoisie and impacted by first-wave feminism and romantic shifts in the notion of the couple, it became an ideal observatory for examining the tensions in modern society. Artists, as much actors in as they were witnesses of these changes, provided sometimes idealized sometimes critical and occasionally deeply ambiguous depictions of them. Based on the Musée d’Orsay’s extensive collections, the exhibition brings together paintings, sculptures, photographs, films, drawings and archives focusing on the many ways of “being a family” in France between 1848 and 1914. From Edgar Degas to Pierre Bonnard, from Victor Hugo to Nadar, from the Lumière brothers to Alice Guy and from Camille Claudel to Rosa Bonheur, these works tell stories of love, filiation, transmission, domination, rivalry and emancipation. The exhibition opens on the inherent links between family and politics, before unfolding in five thematic sections. “Home Sweet Home” explores the house as a place of family embodiment and domestic intimacy, from Degas’, Tissot’s and Bazille’s large-scale portraits of extended families to the destitute homeless families captured by Daumier and Stevens. Rosa Bonheur and the large menagerie she kept in Thomery, as well as the 20th century’s first films portraying emotional alliances between animals and human beings, were already paving the way for alternative models. “Be a mother and keep quiet” focuses on the burden of motherhood and the roles assigned to women. Whether they were mothers or wet nurses, workers or artists, young or in the prime of life, “old maids” or grandmothers, in their flesh and fantasies alike, women experienced pregnancy and breastfeeding, old age and barrenness, adoption, abandonment and the loss of one or more of their children.
